To us Jesus is the shepherd whose flock this was before it was ever ours to keep. He is the one who will ask us what became of the people placed in our care. Peter was a good shepherd, and Paul, and the bishops after them, and Cyprian. Yet to good shepherds he commended one good Shepherd. That is who he is to us.

His death and rising are not facts we simply affirm and set aside. His crucifixion, burial, rising on the third day, ascension, and sitting at the Father's right hand were ordered deliberately. The life we lead here was cut to their shape. We crucify our own flesh: that is his cross in us. We are buried with him in the water: that is his burial in us. We walk in a life made new: that is his rising in us. We set our affection on what is above, our life hidden with him in God. That is his ascension and his sitting at God's right hand, worked out in an ordinary life.

He is also the one who knows what we truly are and meets us there. Augustine told Peter's story with Peter as the sick man and the Lord as his doctor. Peter said he had strength he did not have.

We carried four writings that speak in his own voice -- what we call the four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John -- and letters from the apostles who walked with him or were called by him. We held these to be Scripture, and we held them beside the writings Israel already carried when he walked among us. None of us knew anyone who saw him. No living memory passed hand to hand back to one of his own. That much we cannot give you.

But we did not rest only on confessing it. Augustine pointed to the world itself. Obscure, unlearned men persuaded the whole world of something incredible, by testifying, in writing, that they had seen it themselves. We reason from their testimony, transmitted to us, even though none of us knew any of them.

The same writings also show us the path by which we came to stand where we do. Augustine traced our own bishops' office back to the apostles by name. He counted back from the bishop of Rome in his own day, Anastasius, through Siricius, Damasus, Liberius, and on down the list to Linus, Peter's own successor.

We confess Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord. Then we go on to confess the Holy Ghost as well. That completes the Trinity that makes up the one Godhead. Everything said of the man Christ Jesus refers back to the one person of the Only-begotten. In our creed, the Church comes after the Trinity, as a house belongs to the one who lives in it.

This confession did not go unchallenged. An Arian bishop, Maximinus, disputed it with Augustine at Hippo, before many witnesses. We do not hide that others held differently.

But for us, the question of who Jesus is cannot be split off from the life we actually walk. His crucifixion, burial, rising on the third day, ascension, and sitting at the Father's right hand were ordered deliberately. The life we lead here was modelled on them, not only mystically, but in reality. We crucify our own flesh: that is his cross in us. We are buried with him in the water: that is his burial in us. We walk in a life made new: that is his rising in us. We set our affection on what is above, our life hidden with him in God. That is his ascension and his sitting at God's right hand, worked out in an ordinary life.

When we say he is God's only Son, we are not saying something we hold at a distance from how we live. We are naming the one whose own death and rising became the shape our life is cut to.

The question you have put cannot be answered with one clear rule, because we settled doctrine in more than one way. Sometimes a council met and the bishops present gave their ruling together. Sometimes a bishop wrote on his own authority to his own people or to another bishop. Sometimes Scripture itself settled what was disputed, and a bishop argued from it. And sometimes we held two answers at once, and let them stand.

Our two bishops held different views of what a council can decide. Cyprian opened the council of 256 with words that bound no one. He said we judge no man, and reject no one from communion if he should think differently from us. Augustine held a different rule. But both views rest on a bond neither would break.

When the dispute was between bishops themselves, it was argued by letter and in council, and it could remain unresolved for a long time without breaking our communion. The sharpest example is the font. Cyprian held that nothing valid is given outside the church at all. Augustine held that something real is given even there, though it does no good until the person comes inside. He argued at book length that Cyprian's ruling was wrong. He never once put Cyprian outside our communion.

Scripture stood above every council and every bishop's own letter. About what it contains, there can be no doubt or argument. A bishop's letter can be corrected, and a council can be corrected by a later, greater council, but scripture cannot be corrected that way at all.

For ordinary believers, the main way our teaching reached them was not through councils at all. You were taught before you were washed. We told you what you were joining before you joined it. You said the creed back, and then we baptized you. After that, the regular preaching to the whole church, baptized or still learning, was the main way what we held reached a plain believer.

We read Scripture as the one authority above every council and every bishop's own letter, and we read it to form believers before they come to the water and to keep forming them after. Augustine wrote plainly that the canon of Scripture, Old and New Testament, stands far above every later letter of a bishop. About what it contains, there can be no doubt or argument. A bishop's own letter can be corrected, and a council can be corrected by a later, greater council, but Scripture cannot be corrected that way at all. Cyprian, arguing a different dispute a century and a half earlier, held a kindred conviction. Custom without truth, he wrote, is only the old age of error. Truth is what we owe our obedience to.

We read it out loud, to the whole congregation gathered, baptized and those still learning alike. The same voice works on you again and again. It is not a lecture and not a show. It is the man in charge of you, telling you to your face what he thinks you need. You are taught what you are joining before you join it. We tell you the creed, and the basics of belief, before the water, not after it.

We also drew on Scripture to decide real disputes among us, the hardest questions in the room. Cyprian argued from what the Lord said to Peter when he taught that the episcopate is one. Augustine reached for Paul's own thorn in the flesh to teach that the saints are always heard for their salvation, even when they are not heard as they wished. When crisis pressed on us -- persecution, plague, a rival communion, or Pelagian teaching about human nature -- the system turned it into teaching. Every outside pressure on record reached the ordinary believer changed. It arrived as a sermon, as teaching, or as a decision about who comes to the table.

Scripture was the authority we returned to, and the thing we held we were accountable to. It was not the only thing we held authority in, since our bishops and councils held real authority of their own, over real disputes among us. But it stood above them all.

Augustine wrote plainly that the canon of Scripture, Old and New Testament, stands far above every later letter of a bishop [[lpc.witness.scripture-above-councils]]. About what it contains, there can be no doubt or argument [[lpc.witness.scripture-above-councils]]. A bishop's own letter can be corrected, and a council can be corrected by a later, greater council, but Scripture cannot be corrected that way at all [[lpc.witness.scripture-above-councils]]. Cyprian, arguing a different dispute a century and a half earlier, held a kindred conviction [[lpc.witness.scripture-above-councils]]. Custom without truth, he wrote, is only the old age of error [[lpc.witness.scripture-above-councils]]. Truth is what we owe our obedience to [[lpc.witness.scripture-above-councils]].

We read it out loud, to the whole congregation gathered, baptized and those still learning alike [[lpc.term.preaching]] [[lpc.gravity.preaching-and-catechesis]]. The same voice works on you again and again [[lpc.term.preaching]]. It is not a lecture and not a show [[lpc.term.preaching]]. It is the man in charge of you, telling you to your face what he thinks you need [[lpc.term.preaching]]. You are taught what you are joining before you join it [[lpc.term.catechesis]]. We tell you the creed, and the basics of belief, before the water, not after it [[lpc.term.catechesis]].

We also drew on Scripture to decide real disputes among us, the hardest questions in the room. Cyprian argued from what the Lord said to Peter when he taught that the episcopate is one [[lpc.term.the-one-episcopate]]. Augustine reached for Paul's own thorn in the flesh to teach that the saints are always heard for their salvation, even when they are not heard as they wished [[lpc.witness.heard-for-salvation-not-for-wish]]. When crisis pressed on us -- persecution, plague, a rival communion, or Pelagian teaching about human nature -- the system turned it into teaching [[lpc.core.latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity]]. Every outside pressure on record reached the ordinary believer changed [[lpc.core.latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity]]. It arrived as a sermon, as teaching, or as a decision about who comes to the table [[lpc.core.latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity]].

Scripture was the authority we returned to, and the thing we held we were accountable to. It was not the only thing we held authority in, since our bishops and councils held real authority of their own, over real disputes among us [[lpc.witness.scripture-above-councils]]. But it stood above them all.

We hold ourselves to what the ground actually carries, and we say plainly where it does not. Where a deacon who walked beside one of them tells what he saw, that stands as his telling. Where we name what is missing, that stands too.

What would not survive is anything we claimed but cannot tag to a record. We do not assert what happened in the years our pastoral voice falls silent. We do not give you any lapsed believer's own first-person account of why they gave way. We do not tell you what an ordinary believer felt standing at the font, except the one man who wrote it down himself, years later, already a bishop. We do not name an eyewitness to the risen Lord, or claim a living memory passed hand to hand back to one.

What we do give you is tagged, every claim to its record. A scholar checking those tags would find the record there, cited as it prints itself. Where we draw a link the records themselves do not make — that a bishop's duty to answer for his people is the root of the road back and the font and disagreement kept inside communion — we say plainly it is our own reading.

The thinness is real, and we do not hide it. What survives scrutiny is what we actually have, spoken as what it is, with its gaps named plainly.

The scriptures are what we taught before the water, and what we kept preaching after it, week by week, year after year. For us they were not a book set on a shelf. They were the voice working on you, in the room, again and again, by the man answerable for you.

We taught you the creed before you were washed. You said it back, and then we baptized you. But that was only the beginning. After the water the same voice kept pressing on you, through the scriptures read and expounded. The people were not a silent audience. We put men into office, and we said so out loud. What you heard from the chair was not distant words about distant things. It was the bishop telling his own flock what he thought they needed, to their faces.

Augustine once answered someone troubled by the violence in our older scriptures. As a young man he had been disturbed by the same question: could men who had many wives and did kill men really be called righteous? Once he held our faith, he gave an answer, though not an easy one. Moses showed obedience, not ferocity. God gave the command, and it was righteous retribution, giving to all what they deserved. The same act chosen by a man on his own account would be a different act entirely. He did not stop there. The earthly wars of the old order were themselves a kind of picture, for a time. Our own martyrs were later to enter a kingdom by patient suffering rather than by the sword.

When the scriptures pressed on a living trouble, we answered from them in voice. To one who feared to repent, Augustine wrote: “Whoever you are who have sinned: you hold back from repenting of your sin, because you despair of your salvation. Hear David groaning. Nathan the prophet has not been sent to you. David himself has been sent to you. Hear him crying out, and cry out with him. Hear him groaning, and groan with him. Hear him weeping, and add your tears to his. Hear him set right, and rejoice with him. If sin could not be kept out of you, do not let hope of pardon be kept out.”

The scriptures were not read alone in silence. They were the voice that formed you, in the assembly, under a shepherd who would answer for what became of you.

The one sentence that sits at the centre is this: a particular people has been placed in a particular man's care, and he will answer for what becomes of them. That is not an office he holds apart from the people it names, and it is the root from which everything else we believe about authority grows.

How a man reached that office, in our own record, is told twice and told differently. Cyprian named two things that put him there: the people's suffrage, and God's own judgment. Pontius, his deacon, wrote that the people's favour and God's judgment together made him bishop. Augustine told his own congregation that he came to the office against his own will, chosen by their longing expectation: “But now I imagine that no one has come here except those who want to hear. So I am not speaking to deaf hearts, or to minds that will look down on the word. Instead, this longing expectation of yours is a prayer for me.”

The pattern across both is this: the people act, and the man answers to what was placed on him.

Two theories of authority among bishops stand in our own record, and they are not the same. Cyprian held that no bishop stands over another. Each one judges for himself, and answers to Christ alone. We keep both, because both are ours. We do not claim to have resolved which governs when they pull against each other.

Our bishops traced their own office back to the apostles. Augustine named the line of Roman bishops from Peter to the man sitting in his own day. Cyprian gave the principle that carries that line forward: the ordering of bishops through changes of times and successions carries the church itself. Augustine also said that infant baptism and the refusal to rebaptize came from the apostles, though no apostle wrote either practice down. A custom that old and that universal, held everywhere and founded by no council, is rightly believed apostolic.

The authority a bishop carried was not a rank he held above the people under him. It was an answerability he carried for them. When a member failed, what followed was not a sentence handed down. It was a road walked back, in stages, where the same people who watched the fall were the ones who received the person home. Cyprian wrote to the confessors and asked them to name in each certificate those they had seen themselves, whose repentance was very near complete. The confessors held that their own suffering gave them standing to ask for peace. The church's answer was that the standing was real, and still had to meet something steadier than one man's word: a process examined and walked before the whole congregation.

The bishop's authority reached the people through teaching before it reached them through ruling. You were taught the creed before you were washed. The church that could do that, and call councils of dozens of bishops, was not a gathering anyone had to build. It was already standing.

Authority among us was held inside bonds that disagreement did not break. We keep that as real even where we cannot tell you every case of how it worked. One thing we cannot give you, plainly: how the women among us carried authority in their own words. Numidicus's wife burns beside him. His daughter searches for his body and finds him alive. A community of nuns stands at Hippo in our later years. We know them only through letters our bishop wrote to them and about them. One woman's spoken vision reaches us, Quartillosia's, kept inside a text men wrote. That is one voice, not a body of women's writing.

We cannot say from our own record whether believers regularly hid underground. That question reaches us only as one Roman official's charge, reported in our bishop's reply to him. Demetrianus accused us of causing the wars, plague, and famine troubling the world, by refusing to worship the old gods. Cyprian wrote a whole reply to it. We have failed people, and we will fail again. Your question is honest, and we owe you the same honesty back.

We can tell you what was decided about a person, and how carefully, and by whom. We cannot tell you what an ordinary believer actually felt walking up to the altar, or standing at the font, or sitting in the congregation on an ordinary week. Almost never, that is. Both of our own voices are otherwise bishops. What comes down to us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an unremarkable person in front of him was feeling.

Our core is an ordinary bishop's care of a local flock, in one place, through the sacraments and the gathered congregation. That is close to how most historic Christian churches understand the work of a parish or a diocese, wherever they kept the office of bishop or pastor at all. We are ancestral to the Western church before that church divided. We are not a claim that belongs to one see's own line of succession.

Augustine named Rome's bishops from Peter down to the man sitting in his own day, Anastasius, and before him Siricius, Damasus, Liberius, and on back to Linus, Peter's own successor. Against a different opponent, he named two chairs the same way: Peter's own seat at Rome and James's at Jerusalem, each still filled in his own day by a living bishop. Cyprian, a century and a half earlier, did not draw up a name list of his own. He stated a principle instead: from Peter onward, the ordering of bishops through the changes of times and successions carries the Church itself forward.

So the line runs, and many churches trace themselves through it. We are the root they grew from, not one branch claiming to be the only heir.

You are taught before you are washed. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. You say the creed back, and then we baptize you. That much is the order we know.

Augustine wrote a guide to catechizing those who came to us asking to be made Christians. It begins with creation and runs down to the church's own present time. It teaches the two commandments on which the whole Law hangs, and the creed. The person learning is to say the creed back, and then the water is given.

What happened week by week, in the room with the person learning, is not ours to give you in any detail. We have Augustine's guide to what should be taught, and we have his sermons preached to the whole congregation, baptized and unbaptized alike. Those sermons were the steady voice working on you, again and again. They were not lectures and not a show. They were the man in charge of you, telling you to your face what he thought you needed.

But what an ordinary person felt in those weeks, or what questions they asked their teacher in private, or how long the process actually took for one person standing in front of us — that is the voice we do not carry. We can tell you what was decided. We cannot tell you what an unremarkable learner was feeling from inside. No text written by an ordinary lay believer about ordinary congregational life as such survives from us. What comes down to us is what a bishop saw and decided, not what the person in front of him was feeling.

So we give you the order: teaching, then the creed said back, then the water. And we give you one other thing Augustine said to the people gathered to hear him, baptized or still learning. That is not the process. It is the bond the process was held inside.

We will name plainly what we can trace and what we cannot. Augustine wrote that refusing to rebaptize someone already baptized among heretics is rightly believed to have come down from the apostles. He said the same of baptizing infants: held everywhere, instituted by no council, and rightly held to have been handed down by apostolical authority. Neither claim rests on a written text from an apostle's own hand. Both rest on the same reasoning: a custom this old and this universal, with no other explanation for its origin, is rightly believed apostolic.

The office of bishop is traced too. Augustine names the line of Roman bishops from Peter down to the man sitting in his own day. Cyprian states the principle that carries that line forward.

Now I will name what we do not trace. Neither of them traces catechesis, the road back, or the teaching before the water to the apostles by name. That gap is real. One more thing is not a traced lineage either. We believe the office of bishop is one, and each bishop holds his part of it for the whole. Cyprian argues that from what the Lord said to Peter. It is an argument from scripture, not a second named succession.

You asked what evidence connects our rituals to the earliest followers. The baptism of infants and the refusal to rebaptize: those we trace by Augustine's test, which is age and universality together. The office itself we trace through Rome's own succession. The road is examined, it takes time, and it is not granted on request. But it is real, and it does not close.

We cannot pretend we know what someone felt as they let go of what held them. What we can tell you is what the decision to join us cost in the world's own terms.

You walked away from the old gods your neighbors still worshipped. That was not a quiet, private choice. The gods were not only home shrines or temple rites. They were woven through the guilds, the festivals, the oath that sealed a contract. To turn from them was to stand apart in the open.

If you had wealth, we told you plainly what it was for. Cyprian wrote a whole treatise on almsgiving, and much of it spoke to believers who had money. He told a wealthy woman in our church that her gains were to be shared with Christ. When captives among our own brethren in Numidia needed ransoming, he gathered a hundred thousand sesterces and sent it to them.

For a married person, we held marriage itself as a real good. Augustine named three things it was good for: children, faithfulness to each other, and what he called its sacrament. But he also taught that separation did not end the bond, and that a wife who married another while her husband lived still committed adultery, even if they were separated. That was a limit, not a counsel of convenience.

And if persecution came, what it asked was not hidden. You were interrogated for the Name, and told to deny it, and some who held firm were killed. We do not make that sound easy. We knew those who gave way under that pressure, and we built a whole discipline to bring them back.

We held it plainly, and we held it hard. Cyprian wrote that there is no salvation outside the Church. He said it of heretics, people who confessed Christ but stood outside. Even a heretic killed for confessing Christ is not helped. He gave the ark of Noah as his picture. If anyone could escape who was outside Noah's ark, then he also may escape who is outside the Church. He did not write of people who never heard of Christ, and we do not claim to know what he would have said of them.

Augustine taught that after the final judgment there are two kingdoms, and the death of the wicked shall abide forever. Many around him found this hard to bear. He called their moan "in vain." He would not let them say the punishment ends. God's mercy is shown not in ending their punishment but in mitigating it or granting them respite from their torments. In these chapters he does not name any person or group as lost.
